Ophthalmology · published research

Corneal injury

One small controlled report described 42% faster corneal epithelial healing after He-Ne irradiation following foreign-body extraction. Animal findings are mixed and include adverse ocular findings in an alkali-burn model.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One small controlled report described 42% faster corneal epithelial healing after He-Ne irradiation following foreign-body extraction. Animal findings are mixed and include adverse ocular findings in an alkali-burn model.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact corneal-injury category contains eight publications from 2011 to 2026: one controlled human report, four rat-tagged reports, one rabbit study, and several cell or tissue experiments. Some publications combine animal and laboratory models, so method counts overlap. The only direct clinical report enrolled 80 eyes after foreign-body removal. No independent clinical replication or deduplicated animal-cohort count is available. Koev et al. 2011

Human and clinical evidence

The conference report compared 40 irradiated eyes with 40 controls after corneal foreign-body extraction. He-Ne light at 632 nm and 0.1 mW/cm² was applied for three minutes. Epithelial healing was observed earlier in treated eyes, and the authors reported a 42% shorter healing period, with p<0.001. This was a small controlled report with limited description of allocation, masking, and follow-up; it does not establish benefit across other injuries or corneal procedures.

Animal evidence

Rat and rabbit alkali-burn studies report earlier wound closure or reduced defect area in some protocols. The rabbit comparison found outcomes comparable with medical treatment. A rat study using 830 nm light reported early closure but also cataract development and increased neovascularization or opacity in treated groups. A combined-light and stem-cell experiment reported improved late opacity measures, but the contribution of light alone cannot be separated.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Cell and tissue experiments report wavelength-dependent changes in corneal cell survival, proliferation, migration, and endothelial responses. Red light sometimes countered blue-light injury, while results varied by wavelength and dose.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols range from 632 nm He-Ne exposure in the clinical report to 830 nm LED, other red or near-infrared light, and polychromatic exposure in models. The human schedule was one three-minute session. Animal dose, timing, injury model, and combination treatments differ, preventing a common dose recommendation.

Interpretation

The human result is a preliminary signal from a single small report, while preclinical findings are mixed and include possible harms. Evidence does not support assuming that laboratory or burn-model effects generalize to routine corneal injuries. A reproducible, independently conducted clinical comparison with defined injury severity and patient-centered outcomes is absent.

Evidence strength in source summaryClinical epithelial healing: Limited signal Animal wound closure and clarity: Preliminary Cell survival and migration: Laboratory only
Publications and records8 publications in the exact source category: 1 controlled human report, 5 animal-tagged reports (rat and rabbit models), and 4 in-vitro or mixed-model tags.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The clinical estimate rests on one small older controlled report with incompletely described allocation and a short healing outcome. Animal wound models are mixed, with one rat report noting cataract and opacity concerns. Cell work supports biological plausibility but cannot establish patient benefit or a reproducible dose.

Publication and study types

  • Method counts overlap because some animal studies also include cell experiments.
  • The clinical report includes 80 eyes.
  • Animal cohorts are not deduplicated across publications.
  • No clinical replication is listed.
